\title{Measuring and Decomposing End-to-End Latency\\
       in a Closed-Loop EEG-Driven Music System}
\author{Kirthan Kulkarni}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Closed-loop systems that adapt music to a listener's electroencephalogram (EEG) have been
demonstrated repeatedly, yet none of the systems we could examine reports a measured
end-to-end latency, even though neurofeedback studies find that feedback effects weaken or
disappear at delays of 0.5--1~s. We present a closed-loop EEG-driven music system built on
consumer hardware and characterise its latency component by component. The system
estimates arousal from a frontal $\log(\beta/\alpha)$ index, maps it onto a nine-level
prompt ladder following the iso-principle, and plays audio from a library of pre-rendered
MusicGen segments. Generation runs $1.05$--$6.27\times$ slower than realtime in every
configuration tested, which motivates the precomputed library; the library reduces
worst-case audio latency from $8.0$~s to $1.0$~s. The deployed end-to-end latency is
$6.5$~s, of which $84.6\%$ is attributable to the analysis path rather than the generative
model. Evaluated against labelled eyes-open/eyes-closed ground truth, the deployed estimator
is dominated by 8 of 9 alternative configurations on both detection latency and information
rate. The architecture admits an analysis-path floor of $0.189$~s and an end-to-end latency
of $0.439$~s, at which the information rate is $1.83\times$ that of the deployed
configuration. We further report four statistical properties of closed-loop EEG data that
bear on study design, including a $6.4\times$ inflation of apparent evidence due to
autocorrelation. All 46 quantitative claims are regenerated from recorded data by a single
script. No claim of therapeutic efficacy is made.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} closed-loop systems $\cdot$ EEG $\cdot$ latency $\cdot$
neurofeedback $\cdot$ music generation $\cdot$ reproducibility

% =============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Music listening is a low-cost, non-invasive means of influencing affective state, and a
growing body of work seeks to make it adaptive by closing the loop through the listener's
brain activity. In such systems, EEG is recorded continuously, an affective or arousal
state is estimated, and the music is adjusted in response. Several systems of this kind
have been built and described~\cite{mindmelody,mindtomusic,ehrlich,neurophone,minimalist},
and the area has been surveyed~\cite{dashagres}.

These systems are typically described as real-time, but the time they take to respond is
rarely measured. This omission is consequential. In neurofeedback, delay is itself an
experimental variable: Belinskaia et al.~\cite{belinskaia} trained parietal alpha with
feedback delayed by 0, 250 and 500~ms and found that sustained post-training change was
negatively correlated with latency and absent at 500~ms, and Asai et
al.~\cite{asai} observed an effect on EEG microstates only at zero delay, with a one-second
delay sufficient to abolish it. A closed-loop music system whose response time is unknown
cannot be placed relative to these findings.

In this work, we build a closed-loop EEG-driven music system on consumer hardware and
measure where its latency arises. The system comprises a four-channel Muse headband, a
frontal arousal index normalised to each listener's baseline, a controller that applies
the iso-principle over a nine-level prompt ladder, and an audio engine that selects from a
library of pre-rendered segments rather than generating music online. We decompose the
end-to-end delay into its analysis and audio components, evaluate alternative estimator
configurations against labelled ground truth, and identify the lowest latency the
architecture can reach.

Our contributions are summarised as follows:
\begin{itemize}
  \item We report a measured, component-wise latency budget for a closed-loop EEG-driven
        music system, and show that the dominant term ($84.6\%$ of $6.5$~s) lies in the
        analysis path rather than in music generation.
  \item We show that the deployed estimator is dominated by 8 of 9 alternatives on both
        detection latency and information rate, and that the architecture's latency floor
        ($0.439$~s end-to-end) is also its most informative operating point.
  \item We demonstrate that, for a controller with a finite prompt space, a precomputed
        audio library is preferable to online generation independently of generator speed,
        and reduces worst-case audio latency eightfold.
  \item We identify four statistical properties of closed-loop EEG data that affect the
        design and analysis of studies using such systems, and calibrate one of them
        against synthetic ground truth.
\end{itemize}

% =============================================================================
\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{Closed-Loop EEG-Driven Music Systems}

Recent systems differ widely in how they decode affect and produce music. MindMelody
decodes valence and arousal with a Transformer-GNN encoder, plans interventions with a
retrieval-augmented language model, and conditions MusicGen-medium on the
result~\cite{mindmelody}; it reports $76.8\%$ valence and $72.4\%$ arousal accuracy
cross-subject on DEAP. Ran et al.\ generate emotional music in real time from
EEG~\cite{mindtomusic}. Ehrlich et al.\ close the loop with synthesised affective
music~\cite{ehrlich}. Velasquez-Pe\~na et al.\ drive Ableton Live from a consumer Muse~S
headband~\cite{neurophone}, and Monroy-D'Croz et al.\ build a minimalist interface on
prefrontal EEG over Lab Streaming Layer~\cite{minimalist}. All of these decode affect with
more sophistication than the single hand-built index used here, and we make no claim of
superior decoding capability.

None of these systems reports a measured, decomposed signal-to-audio latency. MindMelody
gives no latency, inference time or hardware specification, and Monroy-D'Croz et al.\
report no latency and no control condition. Ehrlich et al.\ are a partial exception: they
report a 4~s analysis window at $87.5\%$ overlap (a 0.5~s update rate), select zero-phase
filtering to avoid delay, and tune a feedback parameter against perceived latency, but do
not convert these into an end-to-end figure.

\subsection{Feedback Latency}

Delay is treated as a primary variable in neurofeedback~\cite{belinskaia,asai} and as a
design requirement in interactive music generation; Gesture2Music, for example, reports
30~ms inference against a stated 100~ms interaction threshold~\cite{gesture2music}. The
present work applies the same standard of measurement to EEG-driven music.

\subsection{The Iso-Principle}

The iso-principle holds that music should first match a listener's present state and then
lead it gradually toward a target~\cite{altshuler}. Its supporting evidence comes largely
from fixed, non-adaptive sequences: Starcke et al.\ randomised 107 participants to four
pre-set sequences after a sadness induction and found that the iso sequence produced higher
positive affect and valence ($\eta^2 = 0.08$ and $0.09$) under passive
listening~\cite{starcke}. We return to the implications of this in
Section~\ref{sec:limitations}.

% =============================================================================
\section{System Design}
\label{sec:system}

\subsection{Overview}

The system forms a loop of four stages: acquisition, arousal estimation, prompt selection
and audio rendering. A Muse~2 headband streams four EEG channels at 256~Hz over Lab
Streaming Layer. An arousal index is computed over sliding windows, normalised to the
listener's baseline, and mapped by the controller to one of nine text prompts. The audio
engine plays segments associated with the current prompt and crossfades to a new segment
when the prompt changes.

\subsection{Arousal Estimation}

The frontal channels AF7 and AF8 are averaged. Each window of length $W$ is detrended,
band-pass filtered between 1 and 45~Hz, notch filtered at 60~Hz, and transformed with
Welch's method~\cite{welch} to obtain band powers $P_\alpha$ and $P_\beta$. The raw index
\begin{equation}
  I_t = \log \frac{P_\beta(t)}{P_\alpha(t)}
\end{equation}
is computed every hop $H$ and smoothed with a one-pole filter of time constant $\tau$:
\begin{equation}
  s_t = (1-a)\,s_{t-1} + a\,I_t, \qquad a = 1 - e^{-H/\tau}.
\end{equation}
The smoothed index is standardised against a 120~s eyes-open baseline with mean $\mu_b$
and standard deviation $\sigma_b$:
\begin{equation}
  z_t = \frac{s_t - \mu_b}{\sigma_b}.
\end{equation}
Windows exceeding a 350~$\mu$V peak-to-peak amplitude are rejected and do not update the
smoother. The deployed configuration uses $W = 4$~s, $H = 1$~s and $\tau = 3$~s.

\subsection{Prompt Controller}

The controller quantises $z_t$ onto a ladder of nine rungs, each spanning 0.5 standard
deviations and centred on rung $c = 4$:
\begin{equation}
  k_t = \operatorname{clip}\!\left(c + \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{z_t}{w}\right),
        \,0,\,8\right), \qquad w = 0.5.
\end{equation}
Following the iso-principle, the controller does not move directly to the target rung
$k^\ast$, obtained by applying the same mapping to the target $z^\ast$, but plays the rung
adjacent to the listener's current rung in the direction of the target:
\begin{equation}
  \hat{k}_t =
  \begin{cases}
    k^\ast, & |z_t - z^\ast| \le \delta, \\
    k_t + \operatorname{sgn}(k^\ast - k_t), & \text{otherwise,}
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
where $\delta = 0.35$ is a deadband within which the listener is considered to be at the
target. For relaxation, $z^\ast = -1$.
Each rung corresponds to one text prompt, so the controller's output space consists of
exactly nine strings. A minimum dwell time $D$ prevents a new prompt change until $D$
seconds have elapsed since the previous one.

\subsection{Audio Engine}

Each of the nine prompts has 32 pre-rendered 8~s segments, generated offline with
MusicGen~\cite{musicgen}, for a total of 288 segments (38.4 minutes). When the prompt
changes, the current segment is abandoned and the engine performs an equal-power crossfade
of duration $T_{\mathrm{xf}}$ into a segment from the new rung.

This design follows from two properties. First, because the controller emits only nine
distinct prompts, a library covers its entire output space exactly; re-synthesising one of
nine prompts online would be redundant even with an arbitrarily fast generator. Second, a
streaming generator must play each queued segment to completion, so its audio latency is
bounded by the queue rather than by generation speed:
\begin{equation}
  L_{\mathrm{audio}}^{\mathrm{stream}} \le Q\,S, \qquad
  L_{\mathrm{audio}}^{\mathrm{library}} \le T_{\mathrm{xf}},
\end{equation}
where $Q$ is the queue depth and $S$ the segment duration. In our configuration this
reduces the worst-case audio latency from 8.0~s to 1.0~s.

% =============================================================================
\section{Latency Characterisation}
\label{sec:latency}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}

\paragraph{Generation benchmark.} We measured MusicGen throughput in nine benchmark runs
spanning two GPU tiers (a laptop GPU and a datacenter NVIDIA T4), two inference backends
(Hugging Face Transformers and Audiocraft) and three precision modes (fp32, fp16 with
autocast, and fp16 with half-precision weights), giving 44 configuration cells.

\paragraph{Ground truth for the analysis path.} Estimator configurations were evaluated
offline on a recording with alternating labelled eyes-open and eyes-closed blocks, which
produce a known change in alpha power at known times. Each configuration was applied to the
raw recording, and its reproduction of the deployed pipeline was verified against the
session log ($r = 0.989$; configurations reproducing it below $r = 0.9$ are rejected).

\subsection{Metrics}

The analysis-path latency of a windowed estimator is the sum of the window centroid delay,
the mean hop quantisation delay and the smoother's group delay:
\begin{equation}
  L_{\mathrm{analysis}} = \frac{W}{2} + \frac{H}{2} + \tau,
  \qquad
  L_{\mathrm{total}} = L_{\mathrm{analysis}} + L_{\mathrm{audio}}.
\end{equation}
\emph{Detection latency} is the median time from a labelled state transition to the
estimator crossing the midpoint between the two state means. Discriminability $d$ is the
standardised difference in the estimator's output between eyes-closed and eyes-open
blocks. Because consecutive outputs are autocorrelated, we also compute the number of
independent observations per minute,
\begin{equation}
  n_{\mathrm{ind}} = \frac{60}{H}\cdot\frac{1-\rho}{1+\rho},
\end{equation}
where $\rho$ is the lag-1 autocorrelation of the output. We score each configuration by its
information rate
\begin{equation}
  R = d\,\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{ind}}},
\end{equation}
the $t$-statistic per square-root minute, which governs how precisely a session of fixed
duration resolves a difference in state. Latency alone would favour no smoothing, and
discriminability alone would favour smoothing everything to a constant; $R$ balances the
two.

\subsection{Generation Throughput}

Every one of the 44 configuration cells ran between $1.05\times$ and $6.27\times$ slower
than realtime, with the best case on the datacenter T4. The bottleneck is the sequential
autoregressive decode loop rather than arithmetic throughput: on the T4, fp32 outperformed
fp16 with half-precision weights by a factor of $0.952$, and the ordering fp32 $<$
fp16-half $<$ fp16 held in 6 of 6 cells. Autocast inserts a type conversion at every
operation, a cost that is amortised in large batched training workloads but not in
batch-1 decoding. Between-run variation for an identical configuration reached $1.96\times$
on the thermally limited laptop and $1.18\times$ on the T4, so single-run measurements on
consumer GPUs should be reported as ranges.

\subsection{End-to-End Latency Budget}

Table~\ref{tab:budget} decomposes the deployed latency. The analysis path contributes
5.5~s, comprising 2.0~s of window centroid delay, 0.5~s of hop quantisation and 3.0~s of
smoother group delay. The measured detection latency against labelled ground truth is
$5.67$~s, consistent with the prediction. With a 1.0~s crossfade, the worst-case
end-to-end latency is $6.5$~s, of which $84.6\%$ is analysis.

window centroid ($W/2$, $W = 4$~s) & 2.0 \\
hop quantisation ($H/2$, $H = 1$~s) & 0.5 \\
smoother group delay ($\tau = 3$~s) & 3.0 \\

\subsection{Estimator Comparison}

Table~\ref{tab:estimators} compares the deployed estimator with two representative
alternatives, and Figure~\ref{fig:frontier} shows all ten configurations. Eight of the nine
alternatives are both faster and more informative than the deployed setting, which
therefore does not represent a latency--accuracy trade-off but lies off the efficient
frontier.

eyes-closed blocks.}

\midrule

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig6-estimator-tradeoff.png}
\caption{Detection latency against information rate $R$ for each estimator configuration.
The shaded region contains configurations that improve on the deployed setting on both

\label{fig:frontier}
\end{figure}

The principal cause is the smoother. At $\tau = 3$~s, consecutive outputs are nearly
identical ($\rho = 0.962$), yielding only 1.2 independent observations per minute. The
smoother is therefore simultaneously the largest latency term and the main source of the
autocorrelation discussed in Section~\ref{sec:stats}; reducing $\tau$ improves both.

\subsection{Latency Floor}

A causal streaming estimator has no window centroid or hop quantisation, so its only delays
are filter group delay and smoothing. A second-order design with $\tau = 0.1$~s reaches an
analysis-path latency of $0.189$~s. Table~\ref{tab:floor} combines analysis-path and
crossfade durations and compares each total with the 500~ms delay at which Belinskaia et
al.~\cite{belinskaia} no longer observed a training effect.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{End-to-end latency by configuration, relative to the 500~ms delay of
Belinskaia et al.}
\label{tab:floor}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
analysis path (s) & crossfade (s) & end-to-end (s) & ratio to 500~ms \\
\midrule
deployed, 5.500 & 1.00 & 6.500 & 13.0 \\
retuned, 1.750 & 1.00 & 2.750 & 5.5 \\
floor, 0.189 & 1.00 & 1.189 & 2.4 \\
floor, 0.189 & 0.25 & 0.439 & 0.9 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Two observations follow. First, the dominance of the analysis path is a property of the
configuration rather than of the architecture: at the floor, the crossfade becomes the
largest term. Second, the floor is not a compromise. Although per-window discriminability
falls from $d = 1.99$ to $0.61$, the number of independent observations rises from 1.2 to
41.4 per minute, and the resulting information rate is $1.83\times$ that of the deployed
configuration.

Three caveats apply. Detection latency does not decrease monotonically with the budget:
below $\tau \approx 0.25$~s the estimate becomes noisy enough that threshold crossings are
harder to localise. The eyes-open/eyes-closed contrast is considerably larger than the
contrast expected between adaptive and non-adaptive music. Finally, no session has yet been
run at these settings, so the floor is characterised offline rather than in deployment.

\subsection{Controller Stability at Low Latency}

Adopting a faster estimator also requires changes to the controller. Replaying a recorded
session through the $W = 2$~s, $H = 0.5$~s, $\tau = 0.5$~s configuration produces 591
prompt changes that arrive before the preceding crossfade has completed, because a less
smoothed index crosses rung boundaries frequently. Imposing a minimum dwell $D \ge
T_{\mathrm{xf}}$ guarantees that no change begins before the previous crossfade ends, and
reduces this count to 0. The dwell adds to worst-case latency, which becomes $L_{\mathrm{analysis}} + D + T_{\mathrm{xf}}$.

% =============================================================================
\section{Statistical Properties of Closed-Loop EEG Data}
\label{sec:stats}

\subsection{Autocorrelation}

A 20-minute session yields 1043 valid windows at a 1~s hop. With lag-1 autocorrelation
$\rho = 0.953$, the AR(1) effective sample size
\begin{equation}
  N_{\mathrm{eff}} = N\,\frac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}
\end{equation}
is $25.3$. A test that treats the windows as independent therefore overstates its evidence
by $\sqrt{1043/25.3} = 6.4\times$, enough to turn $p = 0.4$ into $p = 0.05$.
Figure~\ref{fig:autocorr} shows that the index decorrelates over approximately 9~s, a time
scale set largely by the smoother rather than by the listener.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth]{fig2-autocorrelation.png}
\caption{Autocorrelation of the arousal index as a function of lag in a 20-minute session.}
\label{fig:autocorr}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Continuous Audio-Neural Coupling}

Cross-correlating the audio envelope with the neural index over a full session loses
statistical power precisely when the intervention succeeds. A listener who reaches the
target and remains there holds the controller on a single rung, leaving little
controller-driven variation in the audio to correlate. In our first pilot, the listener
occupied one rung for $95.9\%$ of the session and the coupling estimate was $r = -0.054$
($p = 0.795$), although the same estimator recovers a known 6~s lag exactly from synthetic
data. The limitation therefore lies in the outcome measure, not in the estimator.

\subsection{Event-Locked Responses}

Restricting analysis to moments when the rung changes restores power, but introduces a
confound: a rung change occurs because $z$ has moved, and $z$ continues to move afterward,
so a positive event-locked effect arises even when the music has no influence. We
calibrated this confound using synthetic sessions with known ground truth. The estimator
returned $+1.503$ for a simulated responder, $-1.467$ for an anti-responder and $+0.011$
($p = 0.573$) for an unrelated session. A fourth session, constructed with no audio effect
but with rung changes triggered by boundary crossings as in the real controller, returned
$+0.435$ ($p = 0.010$). The pilot value of $+0.412$ is indistinguishable from this pure
confound. Its pre-onset slope ($+0.1292$ z/s, against $+0.0573$ for the confound and
$+0.0012$ for a genuine response) and its peak at onset followed by decay are
characteristic of the confound rather than of a response. A positive within-condition
event-locked effect is therefore not evidence of an effect; only the contrast against a
yoked sham condition is interpretable.

\subsection{Dichotomised Outcomes}

Time spent within a target band is clinically interpretable but discards information about
distance from the band and saturates for listeners far outside it. Simulated against the
measured autocorrelation, it requires an effect roughly three times larger to be detected
than the mean of $z$. We therefore designate mean $z$ as the primary outcome. Under a
crossover design with 10 participants, power to detect a 0.15 standard deviation effect
is $38.8\%$, and 25 participants per arm are required for $80\%$ power.

% =============================================================================
\section{Signal Validation}
\label{sec:validation}

We assess two separate properties: whether the electrodes record cortical activity, and
whether the $\log(\beta/\alpha)$ index tracks arousal.

\paragraph{Cortical signal.} In an eyes-open/eyes-closed recording on the temporal pair
TP9/TP10, alpha power rose $2.13\times$ on eye closure ($d = 1.55$,
$p = 2.8 \times 10^{-23}$). This recording used a 150~$\mu$V rejection threshold, which
preferentially removes eyes-open windows because blinks occur with the eyes open; at the
deployed 350~$\mu$V threshold the two conditions are nearly balanced and the ratio is
$1.90\times$. The effect is significant at every threshold tested, including no rejection.

\paragraph{Index channels.} Because the arousal index uses AF7/AF8 rather than TP9/TP10, we
repeated the recording on those channels (Figure~\ref{fig:alpha}). Alpha power again rose
significantly, by $1.34\times$ ($d = 0.53$, $p = 2.3 \times 10^{-6}$, $6.8\%$ of windows
rejected), or by $1.41\times$ ($d = 0.61$) when the protocol's 3~s settling period after
each instruction is excluded. However, the eyes-closed increase in spectral peak
prominence, which the temporal channels pass clearly, was $1.09\times$ on AF7 and
$1.13\times$ on AF8, below a $1.2\times$ criterion. Alpha power therefore rises on the
frontal channels, but a distinct alpha peak barely emerges. This is consistent with
Monroy-D'Croz et al., whose frontal alpha asymmetry explained $0.40\%$ of signal
variance~\cite{minimalist}.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig0-alpha-validation.png}

\vspace{0.6em}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig0b-alpha-validation-af78.png}
\caption{Alpha power during alternating eyes-open and eyes-closed blocks (shaded). Top:
temporal channels TP9/TP10. Bottom: frontal channels AF7/AF8, from which the arousal index
is computed. The flat segment near 300~s in the lower panel is a stream dropout.}
\label{fig:alpha}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Arousal.} We tested the index on the public DEAP dataset~\cite{deap}, which pairs
32-channel EEG with self-reported affect, using the same feature extractor as the live
system. On AF3/AF4 the index correlated with reported arousal at $\rho = +0.303$
($p = 0.058$) and with valence at $+0.082$. The direction of the arousal correlation was
positive across 7 of 7 independent montages (sign test $p = 0.016$).

% =============================================================================
\section{Reproducibility}
\label{sec:repro}

Every quantitative claim in this paper is regenerated from recorded data by a single
script, which compares each recomputed value with the value stated here and fails on any
disagreement; all 46 claims currently reproduce. This practice identified several defects
that would otherwise have reached the manuscript, three of which generalise to any
pre-registered study with an evolving codebase. First, recordings must be referenced by
name rather than selected as the most recent: a second pilot session silently replaced the
data underlying a dozen claims, five figures and eight tests. Second, synthetic data must
be structurally excluded from analysis: a brief demonstration run once recomputed six
claims from a signal generator. Third, a pre-registration integrity check must not force
its own violation: storing the deviation log inside the hashed file made recording a
deviation fail the check, and the log was moved outside it.

Two data-acquisition defects were also invisible to existing checks. The streaming layer
delivered each packet two to four times, with timestamps stepping backwards between copies,
which downstream code interpreted as electrode failure. Separately, raw timestamps were
stored at a precision that degraded with system uptime, from 8~ms after a fresh boot to
0.25~s after 27 days.

% =============================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Efficacy.} This work makes no claim that the intervention benefits listeners.
The evidence consists of two self-administered, unblinded sessions; no adaptive/sham pairs
have been collected and no participants have been enrolled.

\paragraph{Latency relative to the neurofeedback literature.} The deployed latency is
$13\times$ the delay at which Belinskaia et al.\ no longer observed an effect, and the
retuned configuration remains $5.5\times$ that delay. These findings concern operant
neurofeedback, in which the listener must perceive a contingency, whereas the mechanism
proposed here is the iso-principle, whose evidence comes from fixed sequences without any
contingency~\cite{starcke}. This argument has a consequence: if a fixed iso sequence is
effective, an adaptive system must outperform a fixed playlist rather than silence, which
is the comparison a yoked sham condition provides.

\paragraph{Controller degeneracy.} A controller can operate correctly yet produce no
manipulation. In our second pilot, a ladder of 1.0 standard deviation per rung mapped the
listener to a single rung for the entire 20-minute session, so a yoked sham would have been
acoustically identical to the adaptive condition. Narrowing the rungs to 0.5 standard
deviations restored variation (33 prompt changes across 5 prompts in one recording when
replayed through the revised controller). We recommend that studies of adaptive audio
report the number of prompt changes and distinct prompts per session.

\paragraph{Signal quality and scope.} The frontal channels used by the index produce a
weaker alpha response than the temporal channels and fail the peak-prominence criterion.
All latency results are measured on an eyes-open/eyes-closed contrast with a single
headset, operator and participant.

% =============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a closed-loop EEG-driven music system and a measured decomposition of its
end-to-end latency. Contrary to the common emphasis on faster generative models, the
dominant source of delay was the analysis path, and that dominance proved to be a property
of the configuration rather than the architecture. The deployed estimator was dominated by
8 of 9 alternatives on both latency and information rate, and the architecture's floor of
0.439~s end-to-end was also its most informative configuration. We additionally described
four statistical properties of closed-loop EEG data that should inform the design of
studies using such systems. These results characterise the system's engineering
behaviour; establishing whether adaptive music confers any benefit over a fixed playlist
requires a controlled study with participants, which remains future work.

\section*{Code and Data Availability}

All code, the pre-registered analysis plan, the deviation log and the session artefacts
underlying this paper are available at
\url{https://github.com/kirthankulkarni-bit/Brain-Music-Therapy}. The 46 claims are
regenerated and checked by \texttt{python scripts/verify\_claims.py}, and the figures by
\texttt{scripts/make\_figures.py}. The audio library is omitted for size; its manifest is
included and \texttt{scripts/build\_library.py} regenerates it.

The author used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, for help with software development,
data analysis and drafting this manuscript. The author designed the study, conducted all
recording sessions and takes full responsibility for the content. All quantitative results
were regenerated from recorded data by the verification script described above.
